topic: the VOC's nutmeg monopoly: a real massacre funded a company worth more than Apple and Amazon, before it collapsed from its own corruption
title: The Company That Massacred An Island For A Spice In Your Kitchen
description: The Dutch East India Company's nutmeg monopoly made it briefly worth more than today's biggest tech giants combined, and it secured that monopoly with a real massacre on Indonesia's Banda Islands. Original AI-narrated historical commentary, independently researched, not a reupload of any source video.

hook_candidates.text: A company that massacred an island's population to control a spice sitting in your kitchen.
This 400-year-old company was once worth more than Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon combined.
What made one 17th-century trading company worth $7.9 trillion, more than today's biggest tech giants?
Nutmeg wasn't just a kitchen spice. It was once worth more than gold, and worth killing for.

share_trigger: A viewer sends this to the friend who thinks corporations only became ruthless in the modern age, because they want to prove a 17th-century company invented the playbook.
contradicted_belief: Most people assume a company would never massacre an island's population just to control a spice.
closing_comment: That 'perished by corruption' nickname for the VOC might be the most self-aware company joke in history.

sources.note: Coen led the 1621 conquest; roughly 2,800 Bandanese killed, 1,700 enslaved.
VOC's speculative peak value estimated at $7.9 trillion in today's money.
VOC dissolved in 1799; nicknamed 'Vergaan Onder Corruptie' (perished by corruption).
Nutmeg was widely believed to prevent the plague, driving its extreme historical value.

beats.text: Nutmeg was once worth more than its own weight in **gold**.
beats.broll_query: a single nutmeg seed balanced on a jeweler's scale next to gold coins, dramatic light

beats.text: Europeans believed nutmeg cured the plague, and it only grew on tiny Indonesian islands.
beats.broll_query: a cloaked plague doctor sniffing a nutmeg pendant on a chain in a dim medieval street
a plague doctor shrugging beside a bed of visibly sick patients, dark comedic tone

beats.text: That single spice built the **richest** company that has ever existed.
beats.broll_query: a towering wooden trading chest overflowing with gold coins and ledgers, candlelit warehouse

beats.text: At its 1637 peak, this company was worth about **$7.9 trillion** today.
beats.broll_query: an antique stock certificate glowing brighter than faded modern tech company logos beside it

beats.text: That trillion-dollar figure is disputed, since currency conversion across centuries is inexact.
beats.broll_query: a historian's hand hovering uncertainly over old Dutch guilder coins and a calculator, skeptical

beats.text: To protect that monopoly, this company's own leadership committed what historians now call **genocide**.
beats.broll_query: a Dutch colonial flag being planted forcefully into tropical island soil, harsh shadow

beats.text: In 1621, Jan Pieterszoon Coen's forces killed **2,800** Bandanese and enslaved 1,700 more.
beats.broll_query: a nearly empty tropical village with one lit hut among many burned-out huts, smoke

beats.text: Company records just call it **inventory control**.
beats.broll_query: a colonial-era ledger book with a quill checking off a cargo inventory list, dim candlelight

beats.text: This same company went bankrupt two centuries later, mockingly nicknamed 'perished by **corruption**,' and
beats.broll_query: a company's wax seal cracking apart and crumbling into dust on an old wooden desk
